Key objectives include: • Fuel Evaluation and Comparison: Identify and analyze the most promising alternative fuels based on economic, environmental, and scalability factors, assessing their system requirements, fuel blends, infrastructure needs, and potential deployment in alternative fuel corridors. • Stakeholder Engagement: Incorporate insights and feedback from an executive advisory board consisting of key stakeholders from the rail and fuel industries and policy representatives. 1.5 STRUCTURE OF THE REPORT This report is structured to comprehensively address the objectives and research questions outlined above. It is structured as follows: • Chapter 2, Costs and Lifecyle Emissions for Alternative Fuel Pathways: Presents a comparative analysis of the production costs and lifecycle for each alternative fuel, summarizing findings from TEA and LCA. • Chapter 3, Alternative Fuels in Locomotive Engines: Discusses engine efficiency, compatibility, and emissions when using biofuels providing insights from recent testing and modeling efforts. • Chapter 4, Levelized Cost of Locomotive Energy Systems: Explores the total cost of ownership for different locomotive energy systems, including fuel costs, infrastructure support, and operational considerations. • Chapter 5, Scaling Up Biofuel Use: Assesses regional rail energy demand, biomass feedstock availability, and the potential emission benefits of scaling up biofuel use in the rail sector. • Chapter 6, Health Considerations: Examines environmental health and safety concerns related to the adoption of alternative fuels. • Chapter 7, Future Research Directions: Identifies research needs and outlines recommendations for advancing the commercialization and adoption of alternative fuels in the rail industry. • Appendices: Provide additional data, methodologies, and detailed analyses supporting the report’s findings. 3 By systematically evaluating the technical, economic, environmental, and incentive aspects of alternative fuels, this report aims to inform stakeholders—including the Bioenergy Technologies Office, the rail industry, fuel producers, and policymakers—about the potential pathways for using cost effective alternative fuels the U.S. freight rail sector. The insights and recommendations presented will help guide future research, development, and deployment efforts to improve energy security and efficiency of rail transportation while reducing environmental and cost impacts. 4 2 COSTS AND LIFECYCLE EMISSIONS FOR ALTERNATIVE FUEL PATHWAYS 2.1 FUEL PATHWAYS This study investigates 16 production pathways for generating seven alternative fuel options relevant to the U.S. rail sector: RD, BD, bio-oils, ethanol, methanol, DME, and ammonia. These fuels are derived from first-generation biomass (such as corn and soybean), organic wet waste (including sewage sludge and animal manure), cellulosic biomass (like woody biomass and corn stover), and renewable hydrogen. Brief descriptions of all pathways are provided in this section. Detailed descriptions and block flow diagrams are provided in Huang et al. (2025). Commercial technologies such as transesterification (Bland et al., 2015) and hydroprocessed esters and fatty acids (HEFA), both at a technology readiness level (TRL) of 9, are considered for the production of BD and RD, respectively (Xu et al., 2022). Soybean oil and used cooking oil (UCO) are considered as the feedstocks for these pathways.
